News.title: Where is Ed Kemper now, and why is he called the ‘co-ed killer’?
News.content:
EDMUND Kemper is one of the most notorious serial killers in American history.

His crimes shocked California in the early 1970s and continue to fascinate true crime fans to this day.



Who is Ed Kemper?

Edmund Emil Kemper III was born in California in 1948.



As an adult, he grew to an imposing six feet nine inches tall and weighed in at 280 pounds.

Kemper showed disturbing signs from an early age, killing two family cats as a boy and decapitating his sister’s dolls.

He was just 15 when he shot and killed his grandparents, Maude and Edmund Kemper, at their home.

Kemper later told police he had done it simply to see what it felt like.



He was sent to Atascadero State Hospital as a criminally insane juvenile, but was released on his 21st birthday.

Back in society, Kemper embarked on an 11-month killing spree between May 1972 and April 1973.

His 10 known victims included his grandparents, six female students aged between 15 and 23, his mother and her best friend.

He picked up hitchhiking students Mary Ann Pesce and Anita Luchessa in May 1972, stabbing and strangling them before dismembering their bodies.



In September that year he killed 15-year-old Korean dance student Aiko Koo, choking her unconscious before raping and killing her.

In January 1973 he shot 18-year-old student Cindy Schall before dismembering and decapitating her.

The following month he picked up Rosalind Thorpe, 23, and 20-year-old Alice Liu from the University of California Santa Cruz campus, fatally shooting them both.

On April 20, 1973, Kemper bludgeoned his mother Clarnell Strandberg with a claw hammer as she slept and slit her throat.

He decapitated her and performed sex acts with her severed head before using it as a dartboard.



Kemper then cut out her tongue and larynx and put them in the garbage disposal.

Later that evening, he invited her best friend Sally Hallett over for dinner and strangled her to death when she arrived.

He left a note to the police saying: “Appx. 5.15am Saturday. No need for her to suffer any more at the hands of this horrible ‘murderous Butcher’.

“It was quick – asleep – the way I wanted it. Not sloppy and incomplete, gents. Just a ‘lack of time’. I got things to do!!”

Despite Kemper phoning police to confess his crimes, cops didn’t take his call seriously.



Hours later he called, asking to speak to an officer he knew and confessed to the murders.

Found sane and guilty at trial in 1973, Kemper requested the death penalty.

With capital punishment temporarily suspended in California, he instead received eight life sentences.

Kemper had a reported IQ of 145 and was friends with local police officers, which may have aided him in evading suspicion throughout his murder rampage.



Where is Ed Kemper now?

Kemper, now 77, remains behind bars at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville, California, where he has been held since November 1973.

His health has deteriorated significantly.

He now uses a wheelchair and suffers from diabetes and coronary heart disease.

Kemper’s next parole hearing is not due until 2031, when he will be 82 years old.

He has been denied parole 12 times.



Most recently in July 2024, a California state panel refused his release at a hearing Kemper himself refused to attend.

Santa Cruz County District Attorney Jeff Rosell told the board: “Ed Kemper is still dangerous. He remains a high risk.”

Why is he called the ‘co-ed killer’?

During his murder spree between May 1972 and April 1973, the vast majority of Kemper’s victims were female college students – known at the time as co-eds.

This was a term used for women attending co-educational universities.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

For this reason he has become known as the “co-ed killer”.



Kemper, who was featured in the Netflix documentary series Mindhunter, confessed to eating some of his victims’ flesh cooked in casseroles.

News.title: If hot air was a weapon Starmer would have rearmed Britain – but words don’t win wars, PM
News.content:
IF hot air was a weapon, Sir Keir Starmer would have re-armed Britain.

Russian tyrant Vladimir Putin would be quaking in his bearskin boots. China’s Xi Jinping and the Ayatollahs would take note.





Because, to give Sir Keir his dues, he talks the talk on war and defence.

Defence, in case you missed it, is the “fundamental organising principle” of his Government.

It is his “first thought in the morning, the last at night”.

It is “the pillar on which everything else stands or falls”.

There is no dilemma for Sir Keir. “We are not at a crossroads,” he told Europe’s leaders in February.

“The road ahead is straight and clear: We must build our hard power, because that is the currency of the age.”

That means military might. It is the strength to coerce or deter adversaries through the threat or use of force.

It is ships and submarines that sail, soldiers equipped to fight, fighter jets, missiles and drones that can penetrate deep into an enemy’s defences, and a cyber force poised to switch off the lights in Moscow, Pyongyang or Beijing.



Starmer grasps the Russian threat.

“Putin’s aggression does not stop in Ukraine,” he warned last year.

“Russian spy ships menace our waters. Russian planes enter our airspace. Russian cyber attacks hit our NHS.”

Brazen Kremlin spies smeared deadly nerve agent Novichok around Salisbury.

They put explosive dildos on DHL planes and hired thugs for arson attacks in London.



Last month three Russian submarines were caught lurking over sub-sea cables in British and Norwegian waters.

Starmer is far more coy about the threat from China.

He is diplomatic about Donald Trump’s rants that undermine Britain and Nato.

Yet his is clear on how Europe must respond.



“We must stand on our own two feet and that means being bold,” he told the Munich Security Conference.

“We must be able to deter aggression and, yes, if necessary, be ready to fight.”

He knows how to get there: “We are going to have to spend more, faster”.

He admits that means “hard choices”. He knows he must make them quickly.

“Time and again, leaders looked the other way, only re-arming when disaster is upon them,” he warned.



“This time, it must be different. Because all of the warning signs are there.”

This is all first-rate rhetoric. Hurrah! Give Starmer’s speech writers a round of applause. Now, let’s look at reality.

Starmer leads a nation with the smallest Royal Navy since it was founded by Henry VIII.

It has lost seven warships while he was Prime Minister, including a frigate and a mine hunter that used to be based in the Gulf.

When RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus was hit by an Iranian drone last month, there wasn’t one British warship between Singapore and Gibraltar, for the first time in living memory.



It took three weeks to get HMS Dragon into the eastern Mediterranean — and the first thing it did when it got there was call in to port for repairs.

In Dragon’s absence, the Navy has had to borrow a German frigate, from which they command a Nato taskforce. The other five Navy destroyers — boasting the UK’s best air-defence weapons — are all stuck in port.

One of them, HMS Daring, hasn’t sailed for almost nine years. Similarly, five of the six hunter-killer submarines are also stranded in port.

One was deployed to Australia on a trade mission when the war in Iran erupted.

None were available to defend our shores during a major month long mission in March to track three Russian nuclear submarines probing UK waters.



Meanwhile our nuclear deterrent — the bedrock of Britain’s national defence — has been stretched to breaking point.

Only two of the Vanguard-class submarines are serviceable, which means crews endure six-month patrols to ensure one is always at sea. They were designed for maximum 80-day voyages.

The Royal Fleet Auxiliary, which supports the Royal Navy, has not got enough sailors. The ones it does have are on strike over pay.

On land, the Army has shrunk to just 70,000 trained soldiers — its smallest size for over 200 years. Almost all of its guns have been given to Ukraine.



Only a handful have been replaced. The tank fleet is shrinking by 30 per cent, assuming no more cuts. Its flagship Ajax recce vehicle makes soldiers sick and deaf.

Even training exercises have been slashed.

Army chief General Sir Roly Walker warned global threats climax next year and Britain must ready for war.

How exactly is that going? The Deputy Chief of Defence Staff said the Army would struggle to field a thousand armoured troops to Europe.

The RAF is marginally better. Their Lightning and F-35 B Lightning jets are in action across the Gulf.



But it is unclear how many Typhoons will get the radar upgrades to stay war-ready. The Wedgetail AWACs planes are delayed.

It is unclear if the Government will pursue air-launched nukes. Even the flagship Global Combat Air Programme, Tempest, is in doubt — alarming allies Italy and Japan.

Why? Because Starmer has dodged and delayed the choices he promised to make.

He will say he cut foreign aid last year to accelerate cash for defence.

This is true. It was low-hanging fruit in electoral terms.



Voters do not care about aid. Voters care about health, education and welfare.

The tough choice is guns or butter, a choice between what to take from voters now to make the nation safer tomorrow.

At the moment, Starmer’s answer is nothing: Safety can wait, as welfare buys votes.

This is why he is unable to publish the Defence Investment Plan.

The DIP sets out what weapons get funded and which ones gets axed over the decade. It is vital for UK defence.



It is this gulf between words and deeds that triggered Lord Robertson to accuse the PM of “corrosive complacency” yesterday.

It was a rare attack from a Labour grandee but one that has been a long time coming.

Lord Robertson served as a Defence Secretary in Tony Blair’s government.

He was also the last British Secretary General of Nato, and an author of Keir Starmer’s Strategic Defence Review, which made 62 recommendations when finally published last year.

He accused Starmer of paying “lip service . . . to the risks, the threats, the bright red signals of danger”.



How did the Government respond? How do you expect? Warm words.

“We are delivering on the Strategic Defence Review . . . We are finalising our Defence Investment Plan that we will publish as soon as possible, putting the best kit and technology into the hands of our Forces.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If only words won wars. If only words deterred them.

Unfortunately, they don’t.

News.title: Southport monster guarded by FOUR prison officers amid fears inquiry into attack could trigger him into further violence
News.content:
JAIL security has been increased around the Southport killer — who can only leave his cell accompanied by four prison officers.

Axel Rudakubana is locked up for up to 23 hours a day amid fears the damning inquiry into his attack could trigger him into further violence.





The 19-year-old is serving life with a minimum of 52 years.

This week an inquiry said the 2024 stabbings would have been averted if his parents had reported him.

And his innocent victims — Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and Alice Da Silva Aguiar, nine — were also failed by public bodies, including the police.

Rudakubana, who previously threw boiling water at a prison officer, is held on a “safe systems” regime at HMP Belmarsh in South East London.

That means he can only move around under a secure escort of at least four officers.

A source said: “They are taking no chances with him due to the inquiry and his history of violence.

“Prison officers are frightened of him and rightly so.

“They fear he could make a weapon or try another attack like the one he carried out.



“He is deemed a massive danger so they will only unlock his door when they are mob-handed to make sure they can control him if he tries anything.

“At least one of the officers will have a body-worn camera every time they interact with him as well.

“The inquiry into his attack is seen as a potential trigger, which makes an inmate more dangerous.

“Rudakubana has also not changed at all, despite all the sessions with psychologists and therapists.



“He is seen as likely to commit further attacks in jail.

“It means that he is kept in his cell for 23 hours per day a lot of the time because — due to resources — it takes so many staff to unlock him and takes them away from other duties.”

We told how in May last year a guard needed hospital treatment after being scalded by boiling water hurled by Rudakubana.



The fiend has since been banned from having a kettle in his cell.

But he is allowed to mix with other lags for daily exercise, have visits from an imam, buy canteen treats and has access to a telly and DVD player.

A Prison Service spokesman did not comment.

News.title: Posh club loved by royals and celebs trashed after 20 squatters break in and cause £25k of damage during illegal rave
News.content:
SQUATTERS broke into a private members’ club popular with royals and trashed it during an illegal rave.

Around 20 revellers were inside Raffles in Chelsea, with hundreds more believed to be on their way before police arrived.





Eleven people were arrested on Sunday afternoon at the King’s Road venue in West London, with damage estimated at £25,000.

The squatters are believed to have first broken into The March Hare, a pub across the road currently being renovated.

Owner Richard Wynne said they stole up to £10,000 of booze plus the sound system and then broke into Raffles, which has been shut for a year.

Mr Wynne, 47, was alerted on Sunday morning by builders working at the pub.

Partygoers aged from their 20s to their 50s were spotted going into Raffles, a past haunt of Prince Harry.

Private security sprang into action and stopped most from leaving before police arrived.

Mr Wynne said: “As the police were cuffing people, other partygoers started turning up with invites on text messages and WhatsApp and Instagram messages.”

Raffles director and licensee Hamish Ross, 39, said: “It’s the second time since we closed in January last year that we’ve had people break in, it already happened in November.



“The police inspector who came down said we were lucky we got down there so quickly, because it could easily have got into the hundreds of people.”

He added: “There are a lot of closed business premises at the moment because of all the pressure hospitality is under.

“That leads to people hanging around and looking for opportunities. It seems to be organised. These are people that know what they are doing.”



Raffles, awaiting planning permission for a redevelopment, bills itself as the second-oldest nightclub in the capital.

It has long been favoured by royals and high society and its clientele included Prince William and Kate Middleton before they got married.

Oscar-winner Eddie Redmayne and sprint legend Usain Bolt also partied there, as have Made In Chelsea stars Jamie Laing and Spencer Matthews.

Jonathan Chatfield, boss of enforcement firm Equivo, told The Sun that changes to the law in 2012 had the unintended consequence of effectively legalising squatting in commercial properties.

He said: “We’ve had situations where we’ve gone in on the Monday and people were still comatose from a party on the Saturday.”



A Met Police spokeswoman said: “Eleven people — seven men and four women — were arrested on Sunday, April 12, following reports of a break-in at a disused nightclub in King’s Road, Chelsea.

“It was reported that alcohol and food were stolen and consumed from the premises.

“All 11 people were interviewed by officers and bailed pending further inquiries.”

News.title: Inside Airbnb sex gangs using rentals as pop-up brothels to pimp out escorts…as hosts find home littered with condoms
News.content:
WHEN Victoria Borman tried to open the door of her Airbnb apartment after her guest was supposed to have already checked out, she was surprised to find it was bolted shut from the inside.

Nearly an hour later, when the holiday home owner finally managed to gain access to her property, she was even more shocked to find a couple in flagrante – an escort and her client.



The Sun looks into the suspected rise in Airbnbs being used as pop up brothels and finds tales of semen stained bedsheets, long term rentals and the sexual exploitation of women.

“It was despicable,” says Victoria, of the shocking bedroom scene that greeted her at her pretty Cambridge pad.

“I told them to get out or I’d call the police.



“There was an excessive amount of tissues strewn around and condom wrappers scattered across the floor.

“I had to get my rubber gloves on and give the whole place a deep clean afterwards.”

It is a familiar tale up and down the country – The Sun found examples of Airbnbs being used by sex workers in Doncaster, South Yorks and Bristol, Gloucs too.

Giving a reporter an insight into how sex work operates in Swindon, Wiltshire Police’s Adult Sexual Exploitation team warned Organised Crime Groups or OCGs were nearly always behind the Airbnb operating escorts in the town, who often hail from Poland or Romania.

Victoria, who is a Superhost on the platform, purchased her quaint one bedroom property three years ago thanks to an inheritance from her grandparents and for the most part, it’s been plain sailing.



“I have a mixed bag of guests, from builders in the week that are working locally to couples wanting to spend the weekend in Cambridge,” says the 47-year-old.

“Some guests come to the city to visit family and we welcome families with children – we have Play-Doh and games laid out for them.”

But soon after opening the Airbnb, the married mum of three was warned by staff in the pizzeria below, who had kindly offered to keep an eye on her property, that the current guests were acting strangely, leading to a late check out and surprising sex show.

“We had a really young guy who had booked for about five nights, which was fine,” she says.

“He seemed normal, an everyday type of human being and at first there were no issues.



“Towards the end of his booking, however, the guy from the pizzeria told me there had been quite a lot of in and out activity at the property.”

Operating a brothel is illegal in the UK under the Sexual Offences Act, with the term legally defined by a premises used by more than one person for the purpose of paid sexual services.

There is no national statistic measuring how many Airbnbs are used for prostitution but in 2023, councillors in Cambridge called for greater powers to tackle the problem and in Westminster, central London, it was reported last year that more than 2,600 short-term lets were being investigated for rule-breaking, which included properties being used as brothels.

Airbnb owner Victoria’s pad was targeted for a second time when a couple booked in at the last minute and stayed for less than an hour before trying to secure a freebie stay.

“It was a man in his late 60s and a much younger woman,” says the married mum-of-three.



“After they left he sent me a message saying: ‘The flat is not fit for purpose and there’s no way that we can sleep on the bed, we’ve had to leave and I need an immediate refund’.

“But when we checked the property they had had a cup of coffee before heading to the bedroom – there was semen over every inch of my bedding, condom wrappers in the bathroom bin and someone had used the over bath shower hose along with a sponge, some shampoo and a single hand towel.”

Airbnb agreed the guests shouldn’t receive a refund and Victoria tries to carefully vet every potential client in a bid to avoid similar incidents.



The platform’s rules prohibit the use of listings for sexual services but Victoria thinks they should do more when the problem is reported.

“They ban the guests from the platform but that seems to be about it,” she says.

“They will just go on to set up another Airbnb account.”

On the platform’s chat forum for hosts, one user told how “our guests (three women) turned our house into a brothel”, asking Airbnb for help to kick them out.

“Men were coming in and out and we found them online advertising for our location,” they said.



“We sent all the information to Airbnb support but the only support we had in 24 hours was a message asking for extra information like pictures of condoms and so on.”

Men were coming in and out and we found them online advertising for our location.

In September 2023, Airbnb launched a probe following reports a 29-year-old worker had used a listing for hook-ups with clients for a whole year in Doncaster.

Neighbours had spotted up to 15 men a day visiting the house, with one saying: “We have men parking cars on the curb and urinating in the street after.”

Many examples given in this article are of single sex workers who aren’t breaking the law and in some cases, escorts using Airbnbs manage to successfully fly under the radar.

Amanda Bestwick, who has changed her name for this article, is a 30-year-old former sex worker from the South East of England, saying she never had any problems using the platform.



“I got into escorting in my early 20s through a friend that I was with at university who was doing it and recommended it to me,” she says.

“I needed money for food and rent and I did it for four years.”

Under the radar

“Airbnbs became a natural option because hotels can often flag or restrict sex workers so I didn’t want to get into trouble,” adds Amanda, of Airbnb’s popularity with sex workers.

“I would meet up with the clients regularly beforehand for safety purposes, such as going for coffee, to restaurant dates etc, so I could gauge their behaviour and whether they felt ‘safe’ enough for me to be alone with.

“Using short-term rentals like Airbnbs gave us more privacy – it was only when one client suggested it that I started using them regularly for work, about once a week depending on client bookings.



“It was generally quite straightforward because hosts weren’t aware of the work and myself and the client respected the property and rules.”

What is the law in UK? It is legal to sell and buy sex in all of the UK except for Northern Ireland, where it is illegal to pay for sex

However, many activities related to sex work are criminalised, including soliciting sex and keeping a brothel

If more than one person is available in a premises for paid sex, then that is a brothel – however, if a sex worker works alone, they are not keeping a brothel

There are estimated to be 400,000 Airbnb listings across the UK, with typical characteristics for pop-up brothels said to be a high turnover of male visitors, short bookings of between one and three nights, multiple adverts online for sexual services listing the same phone number and OCGs controlling several locations at once.

The English Collective of Prostitutes, a grassroots organisation of sex workers, reported earlier this year that they had seen a 33 per cent increase in calls to their helpline in the last six months.

Most were related to women starting or restarting sex work due to the increased cost of living.

This goes some way to explain why pop-up brothels look to be an increasing trend – and time will tell whether Airbnb’s zero tolerance policy will succeed against determined OCGs and desperate women.

News.title: Save me the ‘lessons have been learnt’ guff after Southport and Nottingham. Just how many red flags do you need?
News.content:
LOSING a child is the worst pain imaginable.

Except for learning that their death was avoidable. That’s even worse.





Then, piling on even more agony, those responsible for the oversights fail to take personal responsibility and hide behind corporate, “lessons have been learned” PR guff.

Being a grieving parent dealing with the unforgivable failure of those paid to supposedly protect the innocent is unconscionable.

Yet the parents of Elsie Dot Stancombe, Bebe King and Alice Da Silva Aguiar — murdered in Southport by Axel Rudakubana — are enduring it.

So too are the parents of Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar — murdered on the streets of Nottingham, along with grandfather Ian Coates, by Valdo Calocane.

These high-profile cases are the mere tip of a system- malfunction iceberg that is failing the innocent victims of those whose serious mental health issues result in violent behaviour.

When 17-year-old Rudakubana walked into a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024 with murderous intent it was, says the public inquiry into the atrocity, a “clearly signposted disaster waiting to happen”.

It criticised his parents for failing to report his disturbing behaviour, but also youth justice services, mental health teams, police, social services, Amazon for ­selling him knives underage, and other agencies who failed to take responsibility for the case.

That’s a hell of a lot of people who, had they not failed so badly at their job, might have prevented the death of three innocent girls.





Rudakubana had a computer search history that showed he was “fixated on violence” and material “offensively demeaning to women and girls”, had a weapons cache at home, refused to attend appointments with the youth justice services and hadn’t attended school for two years.

How many more red flags do you need?

The inquiry heard that his father Alphonse actively obstructed the efforts of mental health and social services to intervene. But surely they, or the police, had the powers to override him?

‘Clear failures’

Instead, when Rudakubana was found carrying a knife in an earlier incident on a bus, and indicated he wanted to stab someone, police treated it as a safe-guarding issue for him and closed the case.

If they hadn’t, a police search of his home would have discovered ricin and other terrorist material, he would have been closely monitored, and perhaps the Southport tragedy might never have ­happened.

Meanwhile, the inquiry into the random killings of Barnaby, Grace and Ian in Nottingham at the hands of killer Valdo Calocane is yielding painful details of similar alleged failings by supposed “experts” in their field.

Barnaby’s mother Emma responded recently: “They are clearly providing ‘their’ well-rehearsed version of the truth. There’s been arrogance, evasion, deflection and an almost total lack of ability to admit what are clear failures.

“Senior people are the worst . . . if this really is the ‘best’ of our government agencies, God help us all.”



Grace’s father Dr Sanjoy Kumar says “people simply didn’t do their jobs” and has called for the individual doctors who treated Calocane prior to the attack to be held responsible, “as they knew [he] was an evil, violent man” yet “ultimately irresponsibly discharging him back into the community to do harm”.

Indeed, a doctor warned in 2020 that Calocane “will end up killing someone” yet he was discharged two weeks later.

Whether this inquiry reaches the same devastating conclusion as the Southport one remains to be seen, but please, no more “lessons will be learned” platitudes.

Until the system puts the safe-guarding of innocent people above that of the mentally ill with violent tendencies, there will be many more unimaginable tragedies like these.

CELEBS TECH ACTION KATY PERRY has been accused of sexually assaulting Batman actress Ruby Rose in an Australian nightclub. Ruby says: “I was in my early 20s, I’m now 40. It has taken me almost two decades to say this publicly.” Ms Perry’s reps have said the allegations are “not only categorically false, they are dangerous, reckless lies”. Whatever the truth, any celeb in today’s “guilty ’til proven innocent” climate might be wise to wear a chest-mounted GoPro camera at all times.

Donald usually goes for a Whopper

DESPITE the title of US President Donald Trump’s “Truth Social” account, he’s often economical with it.

The repeated claims that Iran wants to make a deal and the war is “over”.

The over-inflated investment boasts. His claim last year that “inflation has stopped”. His assertion that foreign leaders are “emptying their prisons and mental institutions” to send criminals to the US.

His post in July 2025 that the Epstein files were a “hoax” by Biden and Obama.



And his numerous deployments of the word “loser” about people who palpably aren’t.

The list is endless, but none of it seems to concern those who voted for Trump – seen here with a McDonald’s delivery at the Oval Office on Monday – despite knowing full well the kind of p***y-grabber they were getting.

And on top of all that, he’s now posted an AI-generated image, later deleted, of him looking messiah-like while tending to the sick.

Saints preserve us. How much longer can this go on?

As the author Maya Angelou once said: “When someone shows you who they are, believe them the first time.”

KOCH A HOOP ASTRONAUT Christina Koch has posted a video of her dog Sadie’s overjoyed reaction when she returned from her trip to the moon. Cute. Though let’s face it, a lot of dogs greet their owners this way when they’ve simply returned from putting the bins out.

LOAD ON A&E IS SICK

MY 94-year-old mother has a new family nickname – Chumbawamba.

She gets knocked down, she gets back up again etc.

Well, to be accurate, she falls because her dementia makes her think she’s more physically able than she is.

Following her latest fall, we waited a day or two to see if it was just internal bruising, then ultimately decided she needed an X-ray.



And here’s where an upsetting situation was escalated to a traumatic one.

She had to be transported flat, via stretcher, and in our area of South London it seems there’s no system in place where the elderly can be transferred by non-emergency ambulance for a pre-booked X-ray at a health centre.

So a nonagenarian with dementia got taken to A&E, where we spent nine hours in a corridor before being moved to a cubicle once it transpired she had a minor fracture in her pelvis that just needs rest.

The NHS staff were brilliant, but the daily/nightly war zone they’re dealing with could be alleviated greatly with a spot of joined-up thinking at national level.

My mother didn’t need to be there and nor, I’d wager, did 60 per cent of those in A&E who could have been diagnosed/treated at GP surgeries, medical centres, mental health facilities etc.

So it’s welcome news that the Government has announced the deployment of “expert clinical teams” to help NHS leaders to end “corridor care”.

But unless billions are thrown at boosting the social care system, A&E’s arteries will remain clogged.

WHILE Meghan will be securing £185,000 for her appearance at a wellness event in Australia, Harry will be getting a reported £36,800 for a speech on mental health in the workplace.

Given his legal tussles with the Home Office over his UK security arrangements, recent court action against Associated Newspapers, and the latest news he’s being sued by Sentebale, the charity he co-founded, it sounds like he might soon be in need of some mental TLC of his own.

DOZENS of plane passengers were stranded in Milan after missing a flight to Manchester thanks to new EU border checks that led to three-hour queues.



Next time, perhaps get a train to France and board a small boat where no such border checks appear to exist.

News.title: Baby found under floorboards may be 300 years old as funeral set to be held for tot wrapped in newspaper
News.content:
BABY TRAGEDY Baby found under floorboards may be 300 years old as funeral set to be held for tot wrapped in newspaper

THE SKELETON of a baby boy who could have died up to 300 years ago was discovered under the floorboards of a house, an inquest has heard.

Referred to as Baby Auckland in official documents, the remains were unearthed by contractors while renovating a building on Fore Bondgate in Bishop Auckland in July 2024.





The baby was full-term, but it is not clear whether he was a stillborn, County Durham and Darlington senior coroner Jeremy Chipperfield heard at the inquest in Crook.

DNA analysis found the baby was a boy but post-mortem examinations revealed nothing about his death.

However, contractors did find a curious brown twine looped three times around the baby’s neck.

Despite being swaddled in a copy of The Umpire newspaper from 1910 and located in a Victorian-era building, carbon dating suggests the remains date much further back.



The first phase involved determining if the child predated the “nuclear age”, which began in 1945 following the first test of the atomic bomb in New Mexico.

Radiation levels confirmed he was older than that, with later tests suggesting the “most likely date range” for the child’s fleeting life was somewhere between 1726 to 1812.

A local undertaker will work with Durham Police and Durham County Council to perform a funeral later this month.

Baby Auckland will be buried in Bishop Auckland cemetery.



A full inquest will resume on 18 May.

News.title: Putin allies confess love for Donald Trump but 'fear he will launch nuke strike'
News.content:
Putin allies confess love for Donald Trump but 'fear he will launch nuke strike'

Russian state TV host Vladimir Solovyov said he likes Donald Trump 'a lot' as he is 'destroying NATO' - but warned the US president could launch a nuclear strike

Vladimir Solovyov says he likes Trump for 'destroying NATO'

Putin's cronies have praised Donald Trump on Russian state TV - with one admitting "I like him a lot" while at the same time warning his behaviour could push the world closer to a nuclear war.

‌



The remarks came during an exchange on the prime-time programme Sunday Evening with Vladimir Solovyov, who appeared alongside Director General of Mosfilm Karen Shakhnazarov and State Duma member Semyon Bagdasarov.

‌



The TV host led the praise for Trump but suggested the US president's unpredictability made nuclear escalation impossible to rule out. "No one can guarantee that America won't carry out a nuclear strike against Iran," he said.

‌



View 3 Images Solovyov told the panel he likes Trump 'a lot' (Image: Russian Media Monitor/Youtube)

"I like him, I like Trump a lot," Solovyov told the panel. "He is destroying NATO. It's a harsh version of an American 'perestroyka' (restructuring)."

He added: "He won't calm down until he destroys America, all of his allies and all of his alliances. Trump suddenly realised that weapons are coming to Iran from someplace."

‌



View 3 Images Putin pictured with Vladimir Solovyov (R) who said he likes Trump 'a lot' (Image: Getty Images)

Solovyov's comments came after Bagdasarov warned political turmoil in Israel had pushed the country into a "dead end", arguing the situation was so volatile that talk of a possible nuclear strike against Iran could not be dismissed. "No one can guarantee it won't happen," he said.

Solovyov questioned whether the same nuclear risk could apply to the US under Trump, before insisting he "likes Trump a lot".

‌



View 3 Images The panel warned Trump could launch a nuclear strike against Iran (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Bagdasarov took a harsher line, describing Trump as a "crackpot" and saying "God only knows what's going on in his head", while arguing Israel was more likely than any other power to escalate towards nuclear action.

Last month, Soloyov warned of an "end times" nuclear war sparked by ongoing tensions in the Middle East.

Article continues below

"With what is happening in America it is clear that nuclear weapons will be used," Solovyov told guests on his show. "Trump is already talking about it openly. I've been talking about it for several years. If we keep thinking 'No, it isn't possible,' it won't help us.

"The scariest thing that will happen is that Trump will use nuclear weapons and understand that this is not a cure-all," he added. "The size of Iran as a country is such that regardless of what kind of nuclear weapons you use… afterwards Iran would respond and the last restriction will fall."

News.title: Tragedy as mum Claire Boland who made desperate 'last resort' plea five months ago dies
News.content:
Tragedy as mum Claire Boland who made desperate 'last resort' plea five months ago dies

Claire Boland, from Stockport, Greater Manchester, had been waiting more than five years for a kidney transplant due to her rare blood combination - and the situation became dire last year

View 3 Images Claire Boland has died after suffering a bleed on the brain (Image: Claire Boland)

A courageous mother who waited more than five years for a kidney donor has tragically passed away.

Claire Boland, from Stockport, Greater Manchester, suffered a "catastrophic" bleed on the brain before losing her life on Saturday April 4. She said last year she had "lost all hope" in the find a suitable match for a kidney, as her rare blood type meant her chances were two in every 10,000 people.

Friends, family and loved ones all came forward to be tested, yet none proved compatible. She suffered a brain bleed while out at bingo with her mum and best friend. It has not yet been confirmed whether the bleed on Claire's brain and her previous health complications are connected.

She leaves behind her husband Damien, daughters Ileana, two, and Elodie, 13, along with her wider family, reports the Manchester Evening News.

Major organ donor development headed by team that saved Mirror boy Max Johnson READ MORE :

View 3 Images Claire, husband Damien, and their children, two-year-old Ileana and 12-year-old Elodie (Image: Claire Boland)

Claire made a desperate public appeal for a donor just five months ago. She was first diagnosed with type one diabetes at just eight years old, which led to a childhood spent in and out of hospital for 'weeks on end'.

Around seven years ago, she developed kidney failure that 'quickly became end-stage'. Claire endured gruelling sessions of haemodialysis, monthly iron transfusions and frequent visits to the doctor for high blood pressure — all on top of managing her diabetes. "It's the not knowing that's so affecting." Claire said in November. "It's such a strain on my mental health... my marriage, my children. I spend my days going to and from the hospital for all sorts of different appointments. I don't feel like I have a life anymore. My life is dialysis."

A desperate Claire admitted: "Putting out this call is my last resort. I feel like it's all on me now to find a donor because I'm just having no luck with the transplant and living donor lists. I don't have any hope anymore. I'm just pleading with people to come forward and get tested."

Heartbreakingly, a matching donor was never found. Claire's mum Deborah Kershaw recalled: "We went to bingo on March 29 and everything was fine... she was fine. We got a drink and sat down. She was just chatting and laughing with her friend.

"She then went to order some food, came back, and the bingo started. I think they'd literally shouted about two numbers and she just sort of flinched and shouted 'mum, I've got a really bad headache'. She was scrunching her eyes up and she kept sort of falling forward.

"Then I noticed her face had started to droop a little bit, so I said 'come on, we need to get you home'." Claire subsequently lost all movement in one leg and her left arm, and when she attempted to get to her feet, she collapsed to the ground. Deborah: "The bingo hall manager ran over and we rang 999. They came straight away and we actually knew one of the paramedics because he'd dealt with Claire before on numerous occasions when she'd had funny turns.

"So they got her sorted, got her into the ambulance and rushed us straight to Stepping Hill Hospital. They thought she'd had a stroke. She was still complaining of horrendous pain in her head, just saying it was really hurting, asking for painkillers. Then she started projectile vomiting."

View 3 Images Claire is pictured with her husband Damien (Image: Claire Boland)

A scan revealed a 'quick, catastrophic bleed to the back of her brain'. Doctors explained they were unable to intervene due to the location and extent of the bleeding.

"If they [had have] transferred her to Salford and operated, she would have passed away on the table. If she did survive the operation, they said she would have been completely brain damaged and she wouldn't have been our Claire anymore.

"So she was on a ventilator, keeping her going. She was heavily sedated." Sedation and ventilation were withdrawn on 31 March. Claire continued fighting for four more days.

Deborah said: "Claire being the fighter she is, she fought for another four days and she sadly passed on April 4. It was very traumatic. Just very sudden. You know, everything she's been through, and yet she managed to get through all that, and then it's a bleed on the brain." Claire's family has launched a GoFundMe page to help cover her funeral expenses and support Damien and their daughters.

What Kidney Donors Need to Know: Before, During and After Donation

Deborah said: "Claire didn't have any life insurance due to her illnesses, so it's all been a bit of a struggle." Honouring her daughter's memory, she added: Claire was lovely. She was absolutely amazing. She was always smiling despite her issues. She didn't let anything get her down.

"She had a heart of gold and would do anything for anybody. She always put other people before herself and she lived for her family - her husband and her girls.

"Her main goal was to go on holiday with the girls. Because of dialysis she wasn't allowed to go abroad, so she desperately wanted a transplant so she could take her daughters away and have a normal life with them.

‌



"She was always happy. She didn't let anything get her down. She'd ring me and have a moan like we all do, but she just kept going, kept smiling, kept fighting. She was a true fighter. It's completely destroyed us. She was my rock. She was my world.

"Her brothers and sister are absolutely devastated. They've lost their oldest sister. It's just hard - you don't expect it. You go for a game of bingo and someone ends up losing their life.

"We're just trying to rally around Damien and help with the children with school holidays and things like that. We all work full-time, so we''e trying to arrange who can take time off and help out. We just want to get as much support as we can for Damien and the girls."

Article continues below

To donate to the appeal, click this link.

News.title: Mum given 12 months to live after cancer diagnosis is told four incredible words
News.content:
Mum given 12 months to live after cancer diagnosis is told four incredible words

When Leah Phillips experienced a dry, nagging cough, the mother was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer at the age of 43, despite never having smoked a cigarette

View 2 Images Leah Phillips has overcome cancer (Image: @leah_l_phillips/Instagram)

A mum who was told she had 12 months to live after she was diagnosed with cancer six years ago is now free of the illness.

‌



A medic recently told Leah Phillips: "There is no cancer" — despite her diagnosis six years ago of stage four lung cancer. Leah was 43 at the time, had never smoked a cigarette and maintained a healthy lifestyle.

‌



But when she experienced a dry, nagging cough, the mother of three went to see her doctor and claims she was given several misdiagnoses, such as allergies. Leah went on to lose 17lb and a subsequent CT scan and bone biopsy showed she had cancer — four months after her first symptoms.

‌



She was given the worst news — that her cancer was terminal — in 2020 but now, after defying doctors for five years, Leah, from Louisville, Kentucky, is now cancer-free.

Tragedy as Tommy Verbickas dies aged just 6 after his third cancer battle READ MORE :

View 2 Images The mum, from Kentucky, wants to warn others of the signs of lung cancer (Image: @leah_l_phillips/Instagram)

Speaking today, Leah said: "There is no cancer showing up in my scans, which is something I never thought I'd see." She said she was told only five percent of people diagnosed with stage four lung cancer live for a further five years.

‌



Medics credit Leah's recovery to her stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), which uses highly targeted radiation beams to treat tumors in all parts of the body, and a lobectomy, which is the surgical removal of one of the lobes of her lungs where the primary tumor had been.

Recalling her initial diagnosis, Leah told TODAY.com: "He (a doctor) said, 'You have six to 12 months to live. We hope you're still here with us next Christmas, and you probably should go home and start to get your affairs in order.'

"I was in a state of shock. I was crying. My whole world turned upside down. It's completely gutting. My kids were nine, 13 and 14 years old at the time."

Article continues below

Through biomarker testing done on her lung tissue, it was discovered that a mutation in her EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) gene allowed the cancer to grow despite her never having smoked tobacco.

But Leah must now have a PET/CT scan every 12 weeks and a brain MRI every six months. She is still taking the targeted therapy of the tyrosine kinase inhibitor pill, but noted that it "won't work forever" and when it "stops working" she would "have to be on another form of treatment." Until that time comes, she wants to spread awareness of the disease.

Leah added: "People need to be aware they can get lung cancer even if they never smoke, and if they're under the age of 50, because most people have no clue that that's a possibility."

News.title: RAF fighter jets scrambled over 'suspected Russian bomber approaching UK'
News.content:
RAF fighter jets scrambled over 'suspected Russian bomber approaching UK'

Two RAF Typhoons were deployed today, reportedly over a suspected Russian bomber approaching UK airspace - it follows Defence Secretary John Healey's warning to Vladimir Putin

View 3 Images RAF Typhoon jets were deployed today, according to reports (file) (Image: Getty Images)

RAF fighter jets have been scrambled over concerns of a suspected Russian bomber approaching the UK, according to reports.

‌



Two RAF Typhoons were deployed from RAF Lossiemouth in Scotland today. A Voyager refuelling jet also took off from RAF Brize Norton in Oxfordshire. The planes flew towards Shetland.

‌



According to The Telegraph, an unidentified Russian warplane remained outside British airspace. The Typhoons later returned to their base as the Russian plane did not need to be intercepted. Sources told the publication that the deployment of British fighter jets tracking the Russian aircraft was part of a wider NATO response.

‌



View 3 Images Putin has been testing the UK military in recent weeks with warships and submarines close to British waters (file) (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

This comes after two Russian Bear-F Tu-142 long-range aircraft were intercepted by six Typhoons as they travelled towards the UK in 2020. And in recent weeks Russian warships and submarines have passed close to UK waters.

The UK and allies tracked a Russian attack submarine and two spy submarines loitering over critical undersea cables in the North Atlantic for a month before they retreated, John Healey revealed earlier this month.

‌



A British warship and aircraft were deployed to deter “malign” activity by Moscow in waters off the UK’s northern coast, the Defence Secretary said.

He said Vladimir Putin had sought to capitalise on the world being “distracted” by the Iran war and that he poses “the primary threat to UK security”.

Addressing the Russian president, Mr Healey said: “We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences.”

‌



Mr Healey told a press conference in Downing Street that in the past few weeks – while many eyes were trained on the Middle East crisis – the UK, in partnership with Norway and other allies, responded to “increased Russian activity” in the Atlantic north of the UK.

View 3 Images Defense Secretary John Healey issued a direct warning to Putin (Image: Getty Images)

This involved a Russian Akula-class nuclear-powered attack submarine and two specialist submarines from Russia’s ministry of defence deep sea research programme known as Gugi (Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research), he said.

‌



Mr Healey said: “In response to the Russian submarines, I can confirm that I deployed our armed forces to track and to deter any malign activity by these vessels.

“A Royal Navy warship and Royal Air Force P-8 aircraft alongside allies ensured that the Russian submarines were monitored 24/7.

“The Akula submarine subsequently retreated home, having been closely tracked throughout and we continued to monitor the two Gugi submarines in and around wider UK waters.

Article continues below

“Our armed forces left them in no doubt that they were being monitored, that their movements were not covert, as President Putin planned, and that their attempted secret operation had been exposed. Those Gugi submarines have now left UK waters and headed back north.”

He said 500 British personnel were involved in the month-long operation. The operation saw RAF crews fly more than 50 sorties using P-8 Poseidon submarine-hunting aircraft, with support from allied countries including Norway.

The Mirror has contacted the Ministry of Defence for comment.

News.title: Major UK car seller to shut down within days – more than 50 years in business
News.content:
Major UK car seller to shut down within days – more than 50 years in business

London-based car dealership Cargiant will close for good on April 24 after its owners were unable to find a buyer for the business, which was once massively profitable

View 2 Images Cargiant is set to close down later this month (stock) (Image: Artur Debat via Getty Images)

A British car dealership is set to close within days - it was once the UK's most profitable business selling second-hand motors.

‌



London-based Cargiant will close its site in the capital for good on April 24 after its owners were unable to find a buyer. The company previously had more than 2,000 cars available and was among Britain's busiest used car supermarkets.

‌



The site covers roughly 50 acres and is estimated to be worth around £100m. It sits adjacent to a planned HS2 interchange that will link HS2, the Elizabeth Line, overground and other transport connections.

‌



Cargiant has encountered difficulties in recent years, with directors being compelled to attempt to sell the business and land. The closure follows Cargiant's owners' failure to "secure a viable future for the business".

View 2 Images Cargiant will shut for good on April 24 (Image: Google Maps Street View)

Major UK pet shop enters administration – it has provided for animals since 1999 READ MORE :

In 2025, the firm recorded a £121.2m pre-tax profit following a revaluation of the land. This followed a pre-tax loss of £22.4m in 2023, reports the Express.

‌



In a statement to Car Dealer, a spokesperson said: "It is with great sadness that we announce the closure of Cargiant's retail operations. This decision follows an extensive consultation process with our team, during which we carefully explored all potential options to secure a viable future for the business.

"We would like to sincerely thank our colleagues for their commitment, professionalism, and the constructive way they engaged throughout that process.

"Unfortunately, despite those efforts, we have concluded that the business is no longer commercially sustainable in its current form."

Article continues below

They added: "This reflects a combination of factors, including a continued reduction in the supply of used vehicles, primarily driven by the EV mandate, alongside rising operating costs and increasing complexity within the used car market.

"Cargiant has been a major part of the UK motor industry for more than 50 years, pioneering the used car supermarket model and growing to become the UK's largest independent car dealership.

"Over that time, we have sold more than one million vehicles and supported thousands of people in building careers in the motor industry and beyond."

News.title: Inside Prince Harry and Meghan's 'humbling' tour as they hit back at criticism
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Inside Prince Harry and Meghan's 'humbling' tour as they hit back at criticism

Prince Harry and Meghan have received a mixed reception since landing in Australia for their first tour since 2018, but this time around they have a very different agenda

View 4 Images Harry and Meghan wave to patients, families and staff at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne (Image: JOEL CARRETT/EPA/Shutterstock)

Prince Harry and Meghan have been 'overwhelmed' by their Australia trip so far.

‌



The couple's trip got off to a mixed start with some Australians branding the pair 'irrelevant', while others greeted them with cheers. Following their arrival, Aussies in Sydney told BBC the couple are 'boring', with one resident adding 'I don’t know why they’re coming'. Another Sydney resident sniped: "They are very much about self promotion, they’d probably be my least favourite royals, put it that way."

‌



However, large crowds gathered to meet Harry and Meghan at Melbourne's Royal Children's Hospital, which the chief executive of the hospital called 'extraordinary' and said they had 'made many a day' by stopping to chat with families. Dr Peter Steer said about their time at the hospital: "I think you've seen by the reception, everybody – staff, patients and their families – are very, very excited just to see them and be part of the occasion.

‌



"The fact that they've taken such time and stopped, I think they have made many a day here today for our patients and families in particular. Young parents say if you see me in the hospital, it might be your work day, but it's our worst day. This kind of special time and special occasion changes their day."

Meghan Markle clears up how to address her as £1.4k wellness retreat fails to sell out READ MORE :

View 4 Images The Duchess appears to reassure a shy child (Image: PA)

‌



The couple chatted with patient's and their families, and posed for selfies with children when they arrived at the hospital, including Jasmine Seidl, 12, and her mother. "I think it's something that she'll remember for a very long time and look back on one day," Jasmine's mum said, adding, "It made us smile for a minute. We're not getting many smiles at the moment, but we've got one this morning."

There's no doubt, however, that it will be a very different tour to their last trip Down Under in 2018 when they undertook an official royal tour shortly after their wedding. Rather than state banquets and walkabouts, the pair will travel across Melbourne, Canberra and Sydney visiting veterans, mental-health units and sport facilities. The trip is a mix of commercial and charitable visits, and there will be no public meet and greets in the visit due to “security and costs associated with keeping public order”.

Meghan will be a speaker at a gala dinner part of an event billed as "a girls' weekend like no other" and a question and answer session will take place in a "fireside chat" - VIP tickets will set fans back about £1,700. Harry is set to give a keynote speech at the InterEdge Psychosocial Safety Summit in Melbourne later in the trip. Delegate tickets for the summit, hosted at Melbourne's Centrepiece conference venue, are available for £525, with platinum tickets costing £1,250 and a virtual ticket allowing on-demand access to Harry's speech costing £260.

‌



View 4 Images Harry turns photographer as he takes a selfie with children during the hospital visit (Image: Getty Images)

It is understood some of the profits will be going to the charity Lifeline, which provides 24-hour crisis support and suicide prevention services - it is not yet confirmed if Harry is receiving a fee.

Meghan has also visited a women's centre run by McAuley Community Services for Women, where she took part in serving food for service users, before sitting down with some of them to chat. The pair went to visit the Australian National Veterans Arts Museum together.

‌



And a spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess has told The Mirror that it was always their intention for this trip to be different to their royal tours.

"This visit has been shaped by a genuine desire to reconnect with organisation the Duke and Duchess have long supported, while also meeting new groups whose work reflects the causes they care deeply about - particularly mental health, women's support services, and the veteran community," the spokesperson said.

Hitting back at claims the reception has been mixed, the rep said they have found the warmth of their local fans 'truly humbling'.

‌



"The reception they have received on the ground has been overwhelming. The warmth, kindness and positivity shown by everyone they have met so far has been truly humbling. They are absolutely delighted to be back in Australia and are greatly looking forward to the days ahead," the spokesperson said.

Controversy had previously arisen about whether any taxpayer funding would be used for the visit, with a petition created and signed by 45,000 Australians demanding that the public purse not be spent on the Duke and Duchess's four day trip to the country. The couple's spokesperson called the petition a 'moot point' as 'the trip is being funded privately'.

"I'm not sure what this petition hopes to achieve... Of course, if you wanted to dive into the ridiculousness of this petition as an agenda for spreading misinformation then one could equally hypothesise that there are approximately 26.5 million Australians (99.98% of the population) who haven't signed it, who must therefore agree with the tax-payer picking up the tab for their visit. Of course, that is another stupid assertion to make but hey..."

‌



View 4 Images The couple were all smiles as they arrived at the Australian National Veterans Arts Museum (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Harry and Meghan won't be doing any walkabouts similar to those they would have undertaken as working royals, however, despite the excitement of the public who have met them so far, with insiders citing the costs associated with crowd management as a major reason behind this. "Security and costs associated with keeping public order are always at the forefront of planning," a source has said, with the visit to Australia being "privately funded" the couple's spokesperson told the Mirror previously.

Article continues below

As criticism of the trip began to increase over the last few weeks, a source who knows the couple blasted the 'misinformation' swirling about, telling the Mirror, "The truth is you have a couple heading down under for work. While they're in town, they’re going to check-in on some charitable causes that they have long supported and - in the Duke's case with the Invictus Games - he set-up.

"The couple are critically aware that by just visiting a charity, they can help shine a light on its work - bringing media attention that wouldn't otherwise exist. They don't have to do that," the source continues.

"They could just as easily get paid and head straight back to California. It's an irrational reaction to s*** - can a couple who just want to support some the charitable causes close to them. God forbid they try to do any good in a world that could, frankly, use a little more Harry and Meghan, and a little less sniping from 'Royal Commentators' who make a living by proving hate bait for anyone willing to platform them. It's sad. What a way to make a living."

News.title: Blair and Brown join Starmer to pay their respects to Labour 'legend' minister Phil Woolas
News.content:
Blair and Brown join Starmer to pay their respects to Labour 'legend' minister Phil Woolas

Emotional tributes were paid at the funeral of Labour "legend" Phil Woolas as former Prime Ministers, including Gordon Brown, joined Sir Keir Starmer at St Margaret’s church

View 5 Images (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

Sir Keir Starmer, Sir Tony Blair and Gordon Brown led mourners paying their respects at the funeral of former minister Phil Woolas. Woolas' coffin was brought into the church adorned with a red shirt from his beloved Manchester United. Tributes were paid to the popular Woolas who died from glioblastoma on 14 March aged 66. Hundreds of former colleagues packed St Margaret’s church in Westminster to say their goodbyes to the former Oldham and East Saddleworth MP.

‌



There were tears and laughter and spontaneous applause after his two sons Josh and Jed spoke emotionally about their dad. Their mum Tracey watched in pride as the boys addressed the congregation. Blair said: “Phil Woolas was steadfast: he was courageous, he was an innovator and he was a motivator.

‌



Former Labour MP Phil Woolas dies aged 66 after battle with brain cancer READ MORE :

View 5 Images (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



"You always knew where you stand with Phil. He was great fun and great company I remember once after a poor Prime Minister’s Question I was frazzled and we were in my office.

“There was an array of whisky bottles and Phil said to me: ‘are you drinking them or are you signing them!" He added: "Phil was taken from us much too soon but what can't be taken from us is the spirit he left behind."

View 5 Images Funeral of popular former Labour minister Phil Woolas (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



Woolas famously kept his cool when he was confronted on live TV by Joanna Lumley in a row over treatment of Gurkhas veterans. But they went on to become friends. Former PM Brown said he had a received a letter from Lumley. Despite their clash she described Woolas as “so kind and friendly to me. He was also very funny." In a witty speech Brown said Woolas was “absolutely fabulous."

View 5 Images Emotional funeral of Phil Woolas

Defence Secretary John Healey said: “He was a proud Northerner. He was a leader, a teacher and always Labour.

‌



"He was a principled politician dedicated to the Labour Party since he was 16 - when he first joined."

View 5 Images Tributes paid at funeral of Labour legend Phil Woolas (Image: *)

Lord Mann said: “Phil never saw himself as better than anyone else. He knew how to listen and observe. He had a photographic memory. Thank you Phil for being our friend.”

Article continues below

Steve Morgan, a close friend who had known Woolas for almost 50 years, said: “The huge number of people attending today just shows the high regard Phil was held in.

“He was a true Labour legend and he will be badly missed by his family, friends and colleagues.”

Novo Nordisk, the maker of the popular weight loss drug Wegovy, and OpenAI, known for its AI chatbot ChatGPT, are partnering to accelerate the search for new medications.

The Danish drug manufacturer announced the partnership in a Tuesday press release, noting that the goal was to bring “new and better treatment options to patients faster.”

Novo Nordisk has already made strides in the healthcare industry with its Wegovy pill becoming the first FDA-approved oral GLP-1 drug for weight loss last December.

Within the new partnership, Novo Nordisk will use “advanced AI capabilities” to analyze datasets, identify drug candidates, and speed up the overall timeline from researching a drug to introducing it to patients, according to the release.

open image in gallery Novo Nordisk, the maker of the popular weight loss drug Wegovy, and OpenAI, known for its AI chatbot ChatGPT, are partnering to accelerate the search for new medications ( AFP via Getty Images )

Novo Nordisk has reassured the public that the data being analyzed will be protected and the partnership will be overseen by humans to “ensure ethical and compliant use.”

The drug maker will also use OpenAI’s technology to make its manufacturing, supply chain, and distribution and corporate operations more efficient.

“There are millions of people living with obesity and diabetes who need treatment options, and we know there are therapies still waiting to be discovered that could change their lives,” Novo Nordisk CEO Mike Doustdar said in a statement.

“Integrating AI in our everyday work gives us the ability to analyze datasets at a scale that was previously impossible, identify patterns we could not see, and test hypotheses faster than ever,” Doustdar added.

open image in gallery The Danish drug manufacturer announced the partnership Tuesday, noting that the goal was to bring ‘new and better treatment options to patients faster’ ( AFP via Getty Images )

Pilot programs within the partnership will be fully integrated by the end of the year.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman praised the partnership, saying AI can “help people live better, longer lives.”

“This collaboration with Novo Nordisk will help them accelerate scientific discovery, run smarter global operations, and redefine the future of patient care,” Altman said in a statement.

According to a poll released by health policy organization KFF last November, one in eight U.S. adults said they are taking a GLP-1 drug such as Wegovy and Ozempic for weight loss, diabetes or another chronic condition. Nearly one in five adults said they have taken a GLP-1 drug at some point.

open image in gallery Novo Nordisk has already made strides in the healthcare industry with Wegovy becoming the first FDA-approved GLP-1 oral drug for weight loss last December ( Getty Images )

Results of a study by Cleveland Clinic published last month found 14.6 percent stopped taking weight-loss drugs because of side effects.

The Independent’s Rhian Lubin heard firsthand from patients who experienced devastating side effects after taking Wegovy and Ozempic, including a nurse practitioner who said she woke up to find she was blind in her right eye and a California man whose wife suddenly died after she suffered a series of violent vomiting episodes.

“If someone would have told me there was a chance that a drug I was taking could make me blind, I would never, ever, have taken the first shot,” Diane Wirth, who went blind in her right eye after taking Wegovy for weight loss, told Lubin.

A Novo Nordisk spokesperson at the time did not comment on the plaintiffs’ individual cases when approached for comment by The Independent, but said that patient safety is the company’s “top priority.”

While some patients claimed to The Independent that they were not warned about the life-altering conditions they have experienced when they started taking weight-loss drugs, Wegovy and Ozempic both warn on their websites of changes in vision and severe stomach problems as possible serious side effects.

Sergio Garcia issued an apology on Tuesday for his outburst during the final round of the Masters, which saw him damage the turf after a poor drive on the second hole and subsequently break his driver against a bench.

The incident prompted Geoff Yang, chairman of the Masters competitions committee, to issue a code-of-conduct warning to Garcia on the fourth tee. This conduct policy was a new addition to the Masters this year.

"I want to apologize for my actions Sunday at The Masters tournament," Garcia stated in a social media post. "I respect and value everything that The Masters and Augusta National Golf Club is to golf. I regret the way I acted and it has no place in our game. It doesn't reflect the respect and appreciation I have for The Masters, the patrons, tournament officials and golf fans around the world."

The 2017 champion began his round with a bogey before hitting a weak fade on the par-5 second hole, sending his ball towards a bunker.

In frustration, he recoiled his driver onto the tee, then turned and slammed the club into the turf. Without repairing the damage, Garcia then struck his driver against a wooden bench holding a water cooler, leaving the club's head dangling from its shaft.

( Getty )

Garcia had initially declined to discuss the official's warning, stating after his round, "I’m not going to tell you." When pressed further, he responded, "Next question." He also did not apologize for his behavior immediately after his closing 75, which placed him 52nd among the 54 players who made the cut. "Just obviously not super proud of it, but sometimes it happens," Garcia remarked.

Since his playoff victory over Justin Rose at Augusta National in 2017, Garcia has not secured a top-10 finish in the 29 majors he has played. He has missed the cut in six of his eight Masters appearances since his win. When asked about his performance record, Garcia simply said, "Bad golf," and when prompted for more specifics, he added, "Bad shots."

This is not Garcia’s first brush with controversy; he was disqualified in 2019 at the Saudi International for damaging greens in frustration. His past antics include angrily kicking off his shoe after slipping during a tee shot at the 2001 World Match Play, an incident that nearly saw the shoe strike an official. He also once spat into a cup during a World Golf Championship at Doral following a three-putt.

The PGA Tour has been developing its code-of-conduct policy over recent years, with the Masters being the first tournament to implement it. The PGA Championship is also set to use the policy next month at Aronimink Golf Club. Under the new rules, a second violation during a tournament incurs a two-shot penalty, while a third violation results in disqualification.

Liverpool are charged with producing another Champions League comeback for the ages at Anfield as they look to flip their quarter-final tie with holders Paris Saint-Germain on its head.

Arne Slot’s side are fortunate to have left the French capital only be trailing by two after being outclassed by PSG last week, with goals from Desire Doue and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia proving the difference in a 2-0 defeat.

The Reds responded with an assured win over Fulham on the weekend, in which 17-year-old sensation Rio Ngumoha scored and starred, leading many to plead for Slot to start the electric winger for tonight’s seismic occasion.

But whether he features or not, Liverpool will need everyone firing against the relentless Parisians, who dumped them out of the competition on their way to the title last year.

After their emphatic FA Cup exit at Manchester City 10 days ago, Liverpool’s hopes of silverware now hinge entirely in Europe so this really is boom or bust for their season.

Hugo Ekitike was stretchered off in an early blow to Liverpool’s bid to overturn their Champions League quarter-final tie with Paris Saint-Germain.

Ekitike went down off the ball holding his ankle after suffering a suspected Achilles injury and appeared in some agony.

Liverpool doctors were quick to signal to the bench that the Frenchman wouldn’t be able to continue and that he would require a stretcher to be taken off.

“Ekitike went to control the ball and he sort of slipped over. He looks to be in pain,” said Alan Shearer on Amazon Prime commentary.

open image in gallery Hugo Ekitike went down off the ball ( AP )

“They are saying he has to come off. It doesn't look good at all.”

The Frenchman was replaced by Mohamed Salah on the right flank, making what could be his fourth last Anfield appearance ever if the Reds fail to comeback from 2-0 down in the tie and progress in the Champions League.

Shearer added: “Salah will have been devastated that he didn't start, but you always get a chance - and his is about to come.”

open image in gallery Mohamed Salah came on in Ekitike's place ( AP )

Ekitike spent two years at PSG and had a point to prove to Luis Enrique, who left the striker out of his Champions League squad in 2023/24.

Ekitike started alongside Alexander Isak against the Champions League holders, the first appearance the Swede had made for four months after recovering ankle surgery, but his evening was curtailed after just 30 minutes with Liverpool now fearing their other striker is set for a period on the sidelines.

The injury could have devastating implications for Ekitike that go beyond Liverpool, with the 23-year-old due to feature for France at this summer’s World Cup.

PSG were also dealt a first-half injury blow, with left-back Nuno Mendes limping off eight minutes after Ekitike’s replacement in place of Lucas Hernandez.

Enrique was then forced into another sub after the break after star winger Desire Doue, who scored in the first leg, collided with the advertising board under the challenge of Dominik Szoboszlai.

The 20-year-old briefly tried to continue after receiving treatment but was not moving freely and hobbled off for Bradley Barcola. Szoboszlai, who appeared to push Doue in the back before he went down, apologised as he left the field.

The Walt Disney Co. on Tuesday began layoffs expected to lead to 1,000 job cuts across the company.

Josh D'Amaro, who in February succeeded Bob Iger as chief executive, announced broader layoffs following a move in January to consolidate Disney's marketing division. The cuts are expected to fall across the Burbank, California-based company's traditional television businesses, including ESPN, as well as its movie studio. Employees in product and technology, and in certain corporate functions will also be affected.

“Over the past several months, we have looked at ways in which we can streamline our operations in various parts of the company to ensure we deliver the world-class creativity and innovation our fans value and expect from Disney,” D'Amaro said in a memo to employees obtained by The Associated Press. “Given the fast-moving pace of our industries, this requires us to constantly assess how to foster a more agile and technologically-enabled workforce to meet tomorrow’s needs.”

Disney last went through a round of layoffs soon after Iger returned for a second spell as chief executive office in 2022. The company cut around 8,000 jobs then. As of late 2025, Disney had about 230,000 employees.

D'Amaro, who previously oversaw Disney's lucrative parks division, has been at the company since 1998.

Contraction has recently been a widespread concern in Hollywood. Paramount Skydance has shed 2,000 jobs since the studio was taken over by David Ellison's company, and Ellison has acknowledged layoffs would follow Paramount's planned merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, if the deal wins approval from shareholders and government regulators. Last week, Sony Pictures Entertainment said it would eliminate hundreds of jobs.

Powerball is jumping the pond.

The lottery game that has made millionaires in the United States will expand this summer to include players in England, Scotland and other parts of the United Kingdom.

An agreement was announced Tuesday between the Multi-State Lottery Association, which runs the lottery game, and Allwyn UK, which operates the U.K.'s National Lottery. The deal still must be approved by a U.K. gambling commission.

It will mark the first time a lottery outside the United States will contribute to the Powerball jackpot.

“We're constantly looking for ways to make sure that we're keeping Powerball culturally and commercially relevant,” said Matt Strawn, who heads Powerball and is chief executive of the Iowa Lottery. “And this really is the next natural progression in doing just that.”

The same jackpot amount will be available to players on both sides of the Atlantic with U.S. payouts in dollars and those in the U.K. in pounds.

For players in the U.S., nothing changes, including the $2 cost of a Powerball ticket and the long odds of winning the jackpot of 1 in 292.2 million, Strawn said. But with U.K. players buying tickets, a larger player pool will grow jackpots more quickly.

“Players consistently tell us in survey after survey that faster growing Powerball jackpots is what they'd like to see,” Strawn said. “Not surprisingly, the higher the jackpots grow the more people play the game in a particular drawing. The more people play, the higher sales grow. The higher sales grow, the higher the jackpots get, the more people play."

For U.K. players, Powerball will offer a chance at much larger jackpots than are now available at lotteries in the country and Europe.

The largest Powerball payout was just over $2 billion from a ticket bought in 2022 in California. EuroMillions, a lottery offered across nine European countries and also operated in the U.K. by Allwyn, paid the biggest prize to a U.K. player of £195 million ($265 million) in 2022.

“Our ambition is to bring more games, more innovation and more excitement to The UK National Lottery — and it doesn’t get more exciting than Powerball, with its transformative jackpots and life-changing contribution to good causes,” Allwyn UK Chief Executive Andria Vidler said in a statement.

Although jackpots will be the same in each country, estimated jackpot amounts will be different due to currency conversion rates and because the U.S. advertises prize amounts pretax, unlike in the U.K.

U.K. Powerball jackpots also will be paid over 30 years whereas in the U.S. jackpot winners have a choice between taking their winnings spread over years through an annuity or in cash — nearly all winners opt for cash.

All players will vie for the same jackpot prize, but smaller prizes will be different in the two countries.

Powerball is played in 45 U.S. states as well as Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

In the game, players choose numbers displayed on five white balls numbered 1 to 69 and one number from 1 to 26 on the red Powerball numbered. Drawings will continue to be held Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays.

More than 31 million people play at least one National Lottery game each year across the U.K.

The new agreement won't change how Mega Millions, the other large U.S. lottery game, operates.
